title: Smartphone
summary: A pocket computer, radio, camera and sensor suite.

layers.basics: A smartphone packs a screen, battery, a main circuit board with the processor and radios, a camera, speaker, and sensors into a slab about 7–8 mm thick.
layers.deeper: Most of the volume is battery and display; the circuit board is only about the size of a few postage stamps, folded into layers to save area.
layers.expert: Typical flagship: 6.1-inch OLED, ≈ 3,300–4,000 mAh (≈ 12–15 Wh) Li-ion cell (4,000–5,000 mAh in 6.7-inch phones), 3–5 nm-class SoC with ≈ 10–20 billion transistors (not every vendor publishes a count), multiple RF bands from 600 MHz to 6 GHz plus mmWave, ~7–8 mm thick, ~170–200 g.

facts: ≈ 10–20 billion (not all vendors publish a count)
did_you_know: A modern phone has more computing power than the computers that guided the Apollo missions, by factors of millions.

title: Display (OLED)
summary: An array of millions of light-emitting pixels.

layers.basics: The screen is a grid of tiny coloured light sources, each switched by a small circuit of transistors and a storage capacitor.
layers.deeper: In an OLED, injected electrons and holes meet in an organic emissive layer, and their recombination forms excitons that give off light (electroluminescence); a thin-film transistor backplane sets each pixel's current, scanned row by row.
layers.expert: AMOLED: LTPO TFT backplane, 120 Hz adaptive refresh; PWM dimming at ≥240 Hz; MIPI DSI link at several Gb/s; sub-pixel layouts (PenTile).

facts: ≈ 1000–2000+ nits (small bright areas or HDR highlights; full-screen sustained brightness is lower)

title: Touchscreen
summary: A transparent grid that senses where fingers are.

layers.basics: A fine grid of transparent electrodes over the display senses the tiny change in electric field when a finger comes near.
layers.deeper: Projected-capacitive sensing: a finger steals some of the field between a drive electrode and a sense electrode, so the mutual capacitance at that crossing drops slightly; a controller scans the whole grid many times per second.
layers.expert: Mutual-capacitance Tx/Rx grid with a pitch of a few millimetres; a finger lowers each node's mutual capacitance by only a small fraction (typically well under half), so signals are tiny; sigma-delta readout, noise rejection near charger frequency; interpolation gives sub-mm position.

title: Battery (Li-ion)
summary: Stores roughly 12–20 Wh of energy, depending on phone size.

layers.basics: A lithium-ion pouch cell stores chemical energy that is released as electricity; it takes up half the phone.
layers.deeper: Li⁺ ions move between graphite and a lithium-metal-oxide electrode; protection electronics guard against over-charge and heat.
layers.expert: Nominal 3.85 V, up to 4.45 V (high-voltage); energy density of several hundred Wh/L; ≈ 500–1000 cycles to 80%; BMS handles cell protection, coulomb counting.

title: Main circuit board (PCB)
summary: A multilayer board connecting all chips.

layers.basics: A thin green board whose copper layers connect the processor, memory and radios.
layers.deeper: Phone boards have 8–12+ layers with microvias (HDI); stacked boards save area; components are soldered by reflow.
layers.expert: Line/space ≈ 30–40 µm; impedance-controlled traces for LPDDR and MIPI; any-layer HDI; EMI shield cans over RF sections.

title: Camera module
summary: Lens stack plus image sensor.

layers.basics: Several small lenses focus light on a chip of millions of light-sensing pixels.
layers.deeper: A CMOS image sensor converts photons to charge in each photodiode; colour filters and processing build a full-colour picture.
layers.expert: Pixel pitch ≈ 0.6–1.4 µm; stacked back-illuminated BSI sensors with ADC per column; OIS voice-coil actuators; MIPI CSI-2 at multiple Gb/s.

title: Speaker
summary: A tiny voice coil moving a membrane.

layers.basics: A coil in a magnetic field moves a thin diaphragm to push air and make sound.
layers.deeper: A class-D amplifier drives the coil; the cavity behind it shapes bass response.
layers.expert: Smart-amp with speaker protection (excursion & thermal models); Lorentz force F=B·l·i; MEMS speakers emerging.

title: Antennas
summary: Metal parts of the frame act as antennas.

layers.basics: Radio waves go in and out through thin metal strips and gaps in the phone’s frame.
layers.deeper: Multiple antennas cover cellular, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, GPS; tunable matching networks keep each efficient when a hand touches it.
layers.expert: Inverted-F/loop antennas; aperture tuners; MIMO 4×4; mmWave patch arrays in packages with beamforming ICs; SAR limits ≈ 1.6 W/kg averaged over 1 g of tissue (US, FCC) and 2.0 W/kg averaged over 10 g (EU, ICNIRP); the averaging masses differ, so the numbers are not directly comparable.

title: USB-C port
summary: Power and data connector.

layers.basics: A reversible port carries both charging power and data.
layers.deeper: CC pins negotiate voltage and current with the charger; high-speed pairs carry data.
layers.expert: USB PD up to 20 V/5 A (100 W) or 48 V/5 A EPR; PPS programmable voltage; 24 pins; e-marker cable ID.

title: Vibration motor (haptics)
summary: A moving mass shaken by a coil.

layers.basics: A small weight oscillates to make the phone buzz.
layers.deeper: Linear resonant actuators (LRA) are driven at their resonance (~170–250 Hz) by a haptic driver.
layers.expert: Resonance f₀ = (1/2π)·√(k/m); drive waveforms tuned for ‘click’ feel; Q and ring-down braking pulses.

title: System-on-chip (SoC)
summary: The main chip: CPU, GPU, AI engine and more on one die.

layers.basics: One chip contains the processor cores, graphics, AI engine, image processor and memory controllers.
layers.deeper: A die of ~100 mm² in a 3–5 nm-class process is stacked under the RAM package.
layers.expert: ~10–20 billion transistors; power budget of several watts at peak and less when sustained; DVFS and thermal throttling manage heat.

facts: ≈ 3–5 nm-class (a marketing node name, not a feature size)

title: RAM (LPDDR)
summary: Fast working memory.

layers.basics: Short-term memory that holds the apps currently running.
layers.deeper: Low-power DRAM stacked on top of the SoC with tiny solder balls to save space.
layers.expert: LPDDR5X: 8.533 Gb/s/pin at its 2021 launch, up to 9.6 Gb/s in the current JEDEC standard (some vendor parts run to 10.7 Gb/s); commonly 8–16 GB in flagships; 1T1C cells are refreshed continually, each row at least every 64 ms or so in the usual DRAM convention.

title: Flash storage (UFS)
summary: Long-term storage that keeps data without power.

layers.basics: Holds your photos, apps and files even when the phone is off.
layers.deeper: NAND flash in a package with a controller; talks to the SoC over UFS.
layers.expert: 256 GB–1 TB; 3D NAND ≥200 layers; UFS 4.0: 2 lanes × 23.2 Gb/s (5.8 GB/s interface maximum), with the vendor-quoted sequential read of Samsung's UFS 4.0 at 4.2 GB/s, below the interface maximum; wear levelling and ECC in controller.

title: Power-management IC
summary: Creates every supply voltage the chips need.

layers.basics: Converts battery voltage into many steady voltages, and manages charging.
layers.deeper: Contains buck converters and LDOs, with charging handled by the PMIC or a companion charger IC; dynamically adjusts voltage to save energy.
layers.expert: Multi-phase buck for SoC core (≈ 0.5–1 V, up to ≈ 10 A), switching ≈ 2–5 MHz; battery charging is often a separate charger IC or charge pump (many phones charge at tens of watts, a few at 100 W or more).

title: RF front-end
summary: Filters, switches and power amplifiers for the radios.

layers.basics: Takes signals from the modem to the antenna and back, filtering out other bands.
layers.deeper: Power amplifiers boost transmit; low-noise amps boost receive; BAW/SAW filters pick bands.
layers.expert: PA efficiency ≈ 40–50% at 3 dB back-off; envelope tracking; antenna tuners; dozens of filters for ≥ 30 bands.

title: Cellular modem
summary: Turns bits into radio waveforms and back.

layers.basics: The cellular modem handles the 4G/5G signal, from coding to modulation.
layers.deeper: It does OFDM, MIMO processing and error correction using dedicated hardware.
layers.expert: Multi-Gb/s peak rates; carrier aggregation; LDPC/polar decoders; beam management for mmWave.

title: Wi-Fi and Bluetooth chip
summary: Short-range radios.

layers.basics: Connects to Wi-Fi routers, headphones and watches.
layers.deeper: Wi-Fi uses OFDM in 2.4/5/6 GHz bands; Bluetooth uses frequency-hopping GFSK or π/4-DQPSK.
layers.expert: Wi-Fi 6E (802.11ax) tops out at 1024-QAM and 160 MHz channels; Wi-Fi 7 (802.11be) adds 4096-QAM and 320 MHz channels in the 6 GHz band; Bluetooth LE adds LE Audio; coexistence arbitration shares the antennas between radios.

title: Motion sensors (MEMS)
summary: Accelerometer and gyroscope.

layers.basics: Tiny silicon structures sense acceleration and rotation, so the screen can rotate and games can use tilt.
layers.deeper: A suspended mass changes capacitance when accelerated; gyros use vibrating structures and Coriolis force.
layers.expert: Accelerometer noise density is quoted in µg/√Hz and varies by part and mode; selectable ranges up to about ±16 g; gyro bias instability is quoted in °/h and is far poorer than in navigation-grade gyros; sensor fusion with magnetometer and barometer runs on a low-power sensor hub or the SoC.

title: Passive components
summary: Roughly a thousand tiny parts in each phone.

layers.basics: A thousand or so tiny capacitors, inductors and resistors smooth power and filter signals.
layers.deeper: Most are surface-mount parts as small as 0.4×0.2 mm; ceramic capacitors decouple supply noise near chips.
layers.expert: MLCC capacitance falls with DC bias (up to −80%); inductors in DC-DC converters (≈ 0.47 µH); a flagship phone has several hundred to about a thousand MLCCs.

title: Crystal oscillator
summary: A quartz heartbeat.

layers.basics: A tiny quartz crystal vibrates at a very precise frequency, giving the chips a precise frequency reference.
layers.deeper: The SoC’s 38.4/19.2 MHz clock and a 32.768 kHz real-time clock both use crystals.
layers.expert: Quartz with Q ≈ 10⁴–10⁶, usually run in a Pierce oscillator between its series and parallel resonance with a specified load capacitance; ±10 ppm typical, TCXO ±0.5 ppm; PLLs multiply it to GHz.

title: CPU cluster
summary: A group of processor cores with shared cache.

layers.basics: The part of the chip that runs your apps, with a few fast cores and some power-saving cores.
layers.deeper: Big.LITTLE style: performance and efficiency cores share a cache and swap work to save battery.
layers.expert: 1+3+4 layouts; shared L3 ≈ 8–12 MB; DVFS per cluster; ≈ 3–4 GHz peak.

title: GPU
summary: Hundreds to thousands of simple units for graphics.

layers.basics: Draws the pixels of games and the interface by doing many simple calculations in parallel.
layers.deeper: Shader cores execute the same program on many pixels; tile-based rendering saves bandwidth.
layers.expert: a few TFLOPS FP32 peak on recent flagships (vendor figures vary and many are unpublished); ray-tracing units; shared LPDDR memory.

title: Neural engine (NPU)
summary: Matrix-multiply hardware for AI.

layers.basics: Specialised circuits run neural networks for photos, voice and text efficiently.
layers.deeper: Arrays of multiply–accumulate units with local SRAM reduce memory traffic.
layers.expert: ≈ 15–50+ TOPS INT8; ≈ 10 TOPS/W; supports int8/FP16.

title: System cache
summary: Shared SRAM near the cores.

layers.basics: Fast memory on the chip that keeps recently used data close.
layers.deeper: Last-level cache shared by CPU, GPU and NPU cuts expensive trips to DRAM.
layers.expert: ≈ 8–32 MB SRAM; ≈ 10–30 ns; hit rates determine battery life as DRAM access costs ≈ 100× the energy of a cache hit.

title: Memory controller
summary: Talks to DRAM.

layers.basics: Schedules reads and writes to the RAM chip.
layers.deeper: Reorders requests to keep DRAM rows open and bus busy.
layers.expert: 64-bit LPDDR5X interface ≈ 68–77 GB/s peak (64 bits × 8.5–9.6 Gb/s ÷ 8); real sustained bandwidth is lower; training and calibration of the PHY at boot.

title: Image signal processor
summary: Turns raw sensor data into photos.

layers.basics: Hardware that cleans up raw camera data: removes noise, fixes colour, and stitches HDR.
layers.deeper: Pipeline: demosaic, denoise, white balance, tone map, sharpen; runs at video rates with low power.
layers.expert: ≥ 4–6 Gpixel/s; multi-frame fusion with NPU; local tone mapping.

title: On-chip interconnect
summary: A tiny network joining the blocks.

layers.basics: Wires and switches that let the processor, GPU and memory talk to each other.
layers.deeper: Packet-switched networks-on-chip with quality-of-service for real-time blocks.
layers.expert: AMBA CHI (coherent) and AXI/ACE-Lite (non-coherent or I/O-coherent) links; ≈ TB/s aggregate; arbitration and power gating of idle blocks.

title: CPU core
summary: One processor core: fetch, decode, execute.

layers.basics: A single core executes instructions one after another, but many at once inside via pipelining.
layers.deeper: Out-of-order superscalar cores decode 6–10 instructions per cycle and track hundreds in flight.
layers.expert: AArch64 (ARMv8.x or ARMv9-A, depending on vendor); reorder buffer of several hundred entries (384 in Arm Cortex-X4); ≈ 6–10+ execution ports; L1 of 64 KB or more per cache; sustained IPC typically 1–3, with peaks of 4–8 on favourable code.

title: Instruction fetch
summary: Reads the next instructions.

layers.basics: Pulls the next instructions from memory using the program counter.
layers.deeper: Fetches several instructions per cycle from the instruction cache.
layers.expert: Fetch 24–32 bytes (6–8 fixed 4-byte instructions) per cycle; some cores add a decoded-op cache; next-line prefetch; steered by branch predictor.

title: Instruction decode
summary: Understands each instruction.

layers.basics: Works out what each instruction means: which operation and which registers.
layers.deeper: Breaks into micro-operations and renames registers to find parallelism.
layers.expert: Register renaming removes WAR/WAW hazards; decode width up to 10 on recent big cores; macro-op fusion.

title: Arithmetic logic unit
summary: Does the arithmetic and logic.

layers.basics: Adds, subtracts, compares and shifts numbers.
layers.deeper: Several ALUs per core operate in parallel; each is built from adders and multiplexers.
layers.expert: 64-bit ALU ≈ 1 cycle (≈ 250–300 ps); Kogge–Stone adder in the critical path; separate multiply/divide units.

title: Register file
summary: Fastest storage in the machine.

layers.basics: 31 programmer-visible super-fast storage slots (backed by a few hundred physical ones) that hold the numbers being worked on.
layers.deeper: Multi-ported SRAM allowing many reads/writes each cycle.
layers.expert: 31 architectural 64-bit registers (ARMv8) mapped to ≈ 300+ physical; ≈ 10 read ports.

title: L1 cache
summary: The nearest memory.

layers.basics: A small, extremely quick memory holding the data and instructions in current use.
layers.deeper: Split instruction and data caches; ≈ 3–4 cycle latency.
layers.expert: 64–192 KB each; 4–12 way set-associative; VIPT; ≈ 95–99% hit rate typically.

title: Branch predictor
summary: Guesses where the program goes next.

layers.basics: Guesses which way an if-statement will go so the pipeline stays full.
layers.deeper: Uses history of past branches; wrong guesses flush work (≈ 10–20 cycle penalty on modern cores).
layers.expert: TAGE-like predictors with ≥ 95–99% accuracy; BTB, return-address stack; speculation side channels (Spectre).

title: Pipeline
summary: An assembly line for instructions.

layers.basics: Instructions pass through stages so several are in progress at once.
layers.deeper: Fetch, decode, rename, issue, execute, memory, retire; hazards cause stalls.
layers.expert: ≈ 12–15 stages; out-of-order issue, in-order retire; ROB ensures precise exceptions.

title: Full adder
summary: Adds three bits.

layers.basics: A full adder adds two bits plus a carry from the previous column; 64 of them (cleverly connected) make a 64-bit adder.
layers.deeper: It uses XOR and AND/OR gates: sum = A⊕B⊕Cin, carry = AB+Cin(A⊕B).
layers.expert: About 28 transistors in static CMOS (mirror adder); prefix trees hide the carry delay.

title: NAND gate
summary: The universal building block.

layers.basics: A NAND outputs 0 only when both inputs are 1. Every other logic function can be built from NANDs.
layers.deeper: In CMOS, two PMOS in parallel on top, two NMOS in series on the bottom.
layers.expert: Logical effort of NAND2 = 4/3; delay ≈ 10–20 ps in advanced nodes; layout uses shared diffusion.

title: CMOS inverter
summary: One PMOS and one NMOS: the heart of digital chips.

layers.basics: When the input is high the NMOS conducts and pulls the output low; when low the PMOS pulls it high. Hardly any current flows between switches.
layers.deeper: Voltage transfer curve is very steep around V_DD/2, giving high gain that restores digital levels.
layers.expert: Switching energy ≈ C V_DD² drawn from the supply per full charge-and-discharge cycle (half dissipated on each transition); short-circuit current during transitions; V_M=(V_DD−|V_Tp|+r·V_Tn)/(1+r) with r=√(k_n/k_p), both transistors in saturation; leakage grows as V_T falls.

formula: E ≈ C·V_DD² drawn from the supply per full output cycle (charge and discharge); ½·C·V_DD² is dissipated on each transition

title: FinFET transistor
summary: A transistor shaped like a fin.

layers.basics: The channel is a thin vertical fin of silicon with the gate wrapping around three sides for better control.
layers.deeper: Wrapped gates reduce leakage at short channel lengths; designers pick the number of fins for drive strength.
layers.expert: Fin pitch ≈ 25–30 nm, fin width ≈ 5–7 nm, gate pitch ≈ 45–55 nm; successors: gate-all-around nanosheets (Samsung from 2022 at 3 nm; TSMC and Intel at their 2 nm-class nodes from about 2025); TSMC's 3 nm-class process still uses FinFETs.

title: Silicon channel
summary: A few nanometres of crystalline silicon.

layers.basics: The part of the transistor where current actually flows is a sliver of near-perfect silicon crystal.
layers.deeper: Doped source and drain on both ends, an undoped channel between; the gate oxide just a few atoms thick.
layers.expert: Si diamond lattice a=0.543 nm; channel width ≈ 5–7 nm ≈ 9–13 lattice cells; strain engineering (SiGe) lifts hole mobility.

title: USB-C wall charger
summary: A mains-to-5–20 V converter in the size of a matchbox.

layers.basics: The charger turns 120/230 V AC mains into low-voltage DC, using a high-frequency switching converter instead of a heavy transformer.
layers.deeper: The chain: mains rectifier → switching MOSFET chopping at 50–150 kHz → small flyback transformer for isolation → optocoupler feedback → output stage.
layers.expert: GaN-based chargers are highly efficient at full load, with most losses as heat in the switch, transformer and rectifier (efficiency varies with load and mains voltage); output is typically 5–20 V, up to 48 V with USB PD EPR; USB-PD chip negotiates voltage over CC wire; QR (quasi-resonant) flyback or ACF topologies.

title: Bridge rectifier
summary: Four diodes that flip AC into pulsating DC.

layers.basics: The bridge makes both halves of the AC wave flow the same way; a big capacitor smooths it into DC near the mains peak (≈ 325 V from 230 V mains, ≈ 170 V from 120 V mains).
layers.deeper: Four diodes conduct in pairs; the bulk capacitor sets ripple.
layers.expert: V_pk=√2·V_rms; bulk capacitor ripple ≈ I/(2fC), f = mains frequency; inrush limiter (NTC).

title: Flyback transformer
summary: Stores then releases energy; isolates mains.

layers.basics: A coupled inductor that stores energy while the switch is on and delivers it to the output when off, keeping the output electrically isolated from the mains.
layers.deeper: Primary-to-secondary insulation withstands >3 kV for safety; gapped ferrite core stores the energy.
layers.expert: Energy per cycle ½L_pI_pk²; turns ratio sets reflected voltage; leakage inductance spikes need snubbers; triple-insulated wire.

title: Switching MOSFET (primary)
summary: Chops the high-voltage DC.

layers.basics: A fast transistor turns the high-voltage DC on and off tens of thousands of times a second.
layers.deeper: Gate driver from controller IC; GaN HEMTs switch faster with lower losses.
layers.expert: 650 V rating; R_DS(on) ≈ 100–500 mΩ; switching loss ∝ f; valley switching reduces loss.

title: Feedback optocoupler
summary: Sends feedback across the safety barrier with light.

layers.basics: An LED and a phototransistor in one package pass the output-voltage error signal without a wire connection.
layers.deeper: Isolates mains side from the user side; the controller adjusts switching to hold the output steady.
layers.expert: CTR ≈ 50–300% and ages; TL431 shunt reference on secondary; ≈ 5 kV isolation.

title: Output buck stage
summary: Trims the output to the requested voltage.

layers.basics: A buck stage steps the voltage down efficiently when the phone asks for a lower voltage.
layers.deeper: USB PD Programmable Power Supply lets the phone request the output voltage in 20 mV steps; chargers realise it with secondary-side flyback control or a buck stage.
layers.expert: Synchronous buck with MOSFET bridge, L ≈ 1–4.7 µH, fsw 300 kHz–1 MHz.

title: Electric power grid
summary: A continent-scale machine from generator to outlet.

layers.basics: Power plants, wires, transformers and substations deliver electricity to every outlet, with supply matching demand second by second.
layers.deeper: Seven stages: power plant → generator → step-up transformer → transmission line → substation → distribution transformer → wall outlet.
layers.expert: Synchronous AC grid at 50/60 Hz; frequency is the real-time measure of balance; ≈ 5–8% losses end to end.

title: Power plant
summary: Where fuel, wind, water or sunlight becomes mechanical or electrical power.

layers.basics: A power plant converts energy from fuel, flowing water, wind or sunlight into electricity.
layers.deeper: Thermal plants boil water to drive a steam turbine; concentrating solar power does the same with sunlight, hydro and wind turn turbines directly, and photovoltaic solar skips the spin entirely.
layers.expert: Carnot limit η≤1−T_c/T_h (temperatures in kelvin); combined-cycle gas ≈ 60%; nuclear ≈ 33–37%; typical unit ratings 100 MW–1.4 GW.

title: Generator
summary: A huge synchronous machine turning rotation into AC.

layers.basics: A rotating magnet inside coils of copper induces a voltage by Faraday’s law; the rotor spins at exactly 3000/3600 rpm for two-pole machines.
layers.deeper: The rotor is fed DC to make its magnetic field; three-phase windings in the stator produce the output at ≈ 11–25 kV.
layers.expert: Hydrogen-cooled ≈ 98.5–99% efficient; synchronous reactance and excitation; inertia constant H ≈ 3–9 s underpins frequency stability.

title: Step-up transformer
summary: Raises generator voltage to hundreds of kV.

layers.basics: A large transformer raises the voltage so that long lines carry less current and waste less power.
layers.deeper: Oil-immersed, three-phase; 20 kV in, 345–765 kV out; ≈ 99.7% efficient.
layers.expert: Mass ≈ 200–400 t for 500 MVA; cooling by oil/forced air; insulation (BIL) rated to lightning impulses of ≈ 1–2 MV.

title: Transmission line
summary: Wires carrying power across regions.

layers.basics: High-voltage overhead lines carry power hundreds of kilometres with only a few percent loss.
layers.deeper: Bundled conductors reduce corona; towers keep spacing for insulation.
layers.expert: Losses I²R; surge impedance ≈ 250–400 Ω; Ferranti rise; HVDC for >600 km or undersea.

title: Substation
summary: Switching and transformation yard.

layers.basics: A substation steps voltage down, routes power between lines and houses protective equipment.
layers.deeper: Contains transformers, busbars, circuit breakers, disconnect switches and relays.
layers.expert: Gas-insulated (GIS) vs air-insulated; protection zones; SCADA; reactive compensation.

title: Distribution transformer
summary: The last step down to household voltage.

layers.basics: The grey cylinder on a pole or the green box on the ground steps medium voltage (≈ 11–35 kV) to 120/240 V or 230/400 V.
layers.deeper: A centre-tapped secondary gives 120/240 V in North America.
layers.expert: ≈ 25–2500 kVA; efficiency ≈ 98–99%; no-load losses run 24/7; overloaded units age by insulation hot-spot temperature.

title: Wall outlet
summary: The user’s end of the grid.

layers.basics: Nominal mains is about 100–127 V in some countries (60 Hz, or 50/60 Hz in Japan) and 220–240 V in most others (50 Hz), usually with a protective earth connection.
layers.deeper: Breakers and RCD/GFCI devices protect against overload and shock; plug types vary worldwide.
layers.expert: RMS voltage tolerances ±5–10%; circuit breakers trip magnetically at ≈ 3–20×I_rated depending on type (B, C or D); US GFCIs trip at ≈ 5 mA imbalance, European home RCDs typically at 30 mA.

ext.title: Wikipedia: AC power plugs and sockets

title: How a phone charges
summary: From the wall socket to lithium ions in the cell.

layers.basics: Mains AC is converted to DC, stepped down, and pushed into the battery by the phone’s charger chip, which watches current, voltage and temperature.
layers.deeper: Constant-current phase until about 4.2–4.45 V, then constant-voltage phase while current tapers; fast charging uses higher voltage to keep current manageable.
layers.expert: USB PD negotiation over CC lines sets the voltage (e.g., 9 V/3 A); charge pumps (2:1/3:1) convert at high efficiency (vendor datasheets quote high peaks, for example 98.6% for one TI switched-capacitor charger, with lower efficiency at light load); cell protection and temperature limits dominate the final stages.

steps.title: Rectify the mains
steps.text: The charger’s diode bridge converts the 230 V AC (peak 325 V) into DC held up by a bulk capacitor.

steps.title: Chop and isolate
steps.text: A fast switching transistor chops the DC at tens of kHz and a small flyback transformer passes energy to the low-voltage side while isolating the user.

steps.title: Regulate by light
steps.text: The output voltage is compared to a reference; an optocoupler passes the error across the barrier so the controller adjusts the duty cycle.

steps.title: Negotiate
steps.text: The phone and charger talk over the USB-C CC wire to agree on voltage and current.

steps.title: Convert and control
steps.text: The phone’s charger IC and PMIC convert to the battery voltage and apply constant current, then constant voltage.

steps.title: Ions move
steps.text: Lithium ions travel through the electrolyte and insert into the graphite anode; the BMS watches temperature and cell voltage.

title: How a transistor switches
summary: A voltage on the gate turns a channel on or off.

layers.basics: In an NMOS, raising the gate voltage above threshold attracts electrons to the surface, forming a conducting channel between source and drain.
layers.deeper: Below threshold, a depletion region isolates source from drain; above it an inversion layer forms and current flows.
layers.expert: Switching delay is limited by charging the gate and load capacitance: t≈0.69RC; subthreshold leakage ∝ 10^{(V_GS−V_T)/S}; short-channel devices need multi-gate geometries (FinFET, now gate-all-around) for electrostatic control.

steps.title: Gate low
steps.text: With V_GS=0 the p-type body has few electrons; source and drain are separated by two back-to-back junctions.

steps.title: Raise the gate
steps.text: Positive gate voltage repels holes and attracts electrons toward the oxide interface.

steps.title: Inversion
steps.text: Above threshold, enough electrons gather to form an n-type channel linking source and drain.

steps.title: Current flows
steps.text: A drain voltage drives electrons through the channel; the gate barely draws any current.

steps.title: Complementary pair
steps.text: In a CMOS inverter, the PMOS and NMOS take turns so the output swings fully high or low.

title: Instruction execution: fetch, decode, execute
summary: How a CPU runs one instruction.

layers.basics: The CPU repeatedly fetches an instruction, works out what it means, does it, and stores the result; billions of times per second.
layers.deeper: Pipelining overlaps these steps; branch prediction guesses the path to keep it full.
layers.expert: Superscalar out-of-order cores rename registers, track instructions in a reorder buffer, and retire in program order to give precise exceptions.

steps.title: Fetch
steps.text: The program counter addresses the L1 instruction cache; a few instructions are read.

steps.title: Decode
steps.text: Instructions are translated to micro-operations; register names are mapped.

steps.title: Read registers
steps.text: Operands come from the register file or are forwarded from earlier results.

steps.title: Execute
steps.text: The ALU computes the result; a memory instruction computes an address instead.

steps.title: Memory access
steps.text: Loads and stores go to the L1 data cache, falling through to L2/L3/DRAM on a miss.

steps.title: Write back and retire
steps.text: Results are written to registers and the instruction retires; wrong-path work is discarded.

title: How Wi-Fi sends data
summary: Bits become radio waves, cross the air, and become bits again.

layers.basics: The phone turns bits into a radio waveform, amplifies it and radiates it; the router reverses the steps.
layers.deeper: OFDM spreads bits over many subcarriers; error-correcting codes protect against fades.
layers.expert: Pipeline: scrambler → LDPC encoder → QAM mapper → IFFT + cyclic prefix → DAC → mixer to 5 GHz → PA → antenna; receiver does AGC, sync, FFT, equalise, LDPC decode.

steps.title: Packetise
steps.text: Software splits data into frames and adds headers and a checksum.

steps.title: Encode and map
steps.text: Error-correcting bits are added; groups of bits map onto QAM constellation points.

steps.title: OFDM
steps.text: An inverse FFT combines many subcarriers into one time-domain waveform.

steps.title: Up-convert and amplify
steps.text: A mixer shifts it to 2.4/5/6 GHz; the power amplifier boosts it.

steps.title: Radiate
steps.text: Currents on the antenna launch a wave that reflects around the room.

steps.title: Receive
steps.text: The router’s antenna, LNA, mixer and ADC capture the signal and the FFT/decoder recover the bits.

title: How a photo is taken
summary: Light to pixels.

layers.basics: The lens focuses light onto the sensor; each pixel turns light into an electrical charge, which is read out, digitised and processed into a picture.
layers.deeper: Colour filters make each pixel see only red, green or blue; the ISP reconstructs full colour.
layers.expert: Photon shot noise limits SNR (√N); read noise, full-well capacity and dynamic range; multi-frame HDR fuses exposures; rolling shutter timing.

steps.title: Focus
steps.text: The voice-coil actuator moves the lens; stabilisation compensates shake.

steps.title: Collect photons
steps.text: Photodiodes convert photons into electron–hole pairs and store charge.

steps.title: Read out
steps.text: Column ADCs convert each pixel’s voltage into 10–14 bit numbers.

steps.title: Image processing
steps.text: The ISP demosaics, denoises, corrects colour and tone-maps.

steps.title: Neural enhancement
steps.text: The NPU adds scene detection, HDR fusion and portrait depth.

steps.title: Store
steps.text: The result is compressed and written to flash.

title: Chip fabrication
summary: From sand to a processor.

layers.basics: A silicon wafer goes through hundreds of cycles of adding a layer, printing a pattern and etching it, building billions of transistors.
layers.deeper: Cleanroom steps: grow oxide, coat resist, expose, develop, etch, implant, deposit metal, repeat; then dice and package.
layers.expert: The whole flow is a very long sequence of hundreds of steps: the front-end builds the transistors and the back-end adds many copper metal layers; EUV is used only on the finest critical layers (published tool-planning scenarios range from 5 to 25 EUV layers); yield learning; test, binning and packaging with TSVs and hybrid bonding.

steps.title: Wafer
steps.text: Sand is purified to 99.9999999% silicon, grown as a single crystal and sliced into wafers.

steps.title: Oxidise and deposit
steps.text: Thin insulating and conducting films are grown or deposited.

steps.title: Pattern
steps.text: Light through a mask exposes resist; deep-UV with multi-patterning or EUV prints features below 20 nm.

steps.title: Etch and implant
steps.text: Plasma etching carves fins; ion implantation sets n- and p-type regions.

steps.title: Wire it up
steps.text: Copper interconnects are built layer by layer above the transistors.

steps.title: Test and package
steps.text: Wafers are tested, diced and packaged into chips like the SoC.

title: Power grid delivery
summary: From a power plant to your outlet.

layers.basics: Electricity is generated, boosted to high voltage, sent over long wires, stepped down at substations and finally lowered to household voltage.
layers.deeper: Supply and demand must always balance; frequency tells operators if they do.
layers.expert: Steady-state AC grids are synchronised; power flows follow impedance, not contracts; contingency planning (N−1) protects against single failures.

steps.title: Generate
steps.text: Turbines spin generators producing AC at about 20 kV.

steps.title: Step up
steps.text: A transformer raises the voltage to hundreds of kV, reducing current.

steps.title: Transmit
steps.text: Overhead lines carry power across regions.

steps.title: Step down
steps.text: Substations reduce the voltage and split power among feeders.

steps.title: Distribute
steps.text: Local lines carry 11–35 kV to the street.

steps.title: Deliver
steps.text: The final transformer provides 120/230 V to the outlet.

title: How a touchscreen senses touch
summary: A finger changes capacitance.

layers.basics: A grid of electrodes lies under the glass; a finger nearby changes the electric field, and the controller finds where.
layers.deeper: The controller drives rows and senses columns; a touch reduces the mutual capacitance at the crossing.
layers.expert: ΔC/C is a small fraction of the node capacitance; noise from display and charger is filtered; palm rejection; hover sensing; stylus uses active signalling.

steps.title: Drive
steps.text: The controller sends a signal on each row electrode in turn.

steps.title: Couple
steps.text: The signal couples capacitively to the column electrodes across each crossing.

steps.title: Finger perturbs
steps.text: A finger diverts some field lines to the body, reducing the coupled signal at nearby crossings.

steps.title: Measure
steps.text: Sense circuits digitise each node’s change.

steps.title: Locate
steps.text: The controller interpolates between nodes to get sub-millimetre position and reports it.
